newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Two French soldiers killed in Bangui.
newsitem.headline: Two French soldiers killed in Bangui.

text.p: Army mutineers in the Central African Republic shot dead two unarmed French soldiers "in cold blood" in the capital Bangui on Saturday during a lull in fierce battles between the two sides, witnesses said.

Sources close to efforts to defuse the impoverished nation's third army revolt within a year told Reuters the two soldiers had been part of a multi-national team visiting a barricade where a 22-year-old protester was killed earlier.

Witnesses reported a mutineer opening fire on the soldiers, whose visit to the barricade came during a tense morning lull that followed clashes between French troops, mutineers and civilian protesters who support them.

One source said the two were shot dead "in cold blood" at the barricade in the rebel-held La Kouanga suburb where the team, which included officers from Chad and Burkina Faso, had gone at the request of the mutineers.
"It was a peaceful operation," that source added.

Witnesses said French troops, who intervened in an earlier army revolt in May to keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power, had reinforced, deploying tanks and armoured personnel carriers in the city. French helicopters hovered overhead.
In Paris, the Defence Ministry condemned the killings as a "cowardly murder" and said the two had been working for a committee set up by four African leaders to consolidate a truce.

"France reiterates its support for the action of this committee of African heads of state and will not tolerate such attacks against its soldiers, who are working for peace and democracy," it said in a statement.
Mediation efforts continued. "We are continuing our efforts," Colonel Alioune Ibaba, Gabonese coordinator of the follow-up committee, told Reuters.
French sources, quoted by Radio France International, said French troops intervened early on Saturday after youths had attacked homes and business of foreigners.
Witnesses said French troops fired teargas and shots in the air to disperse civilians, who tried overnight to advance down Avenue Boganda, Bangui's main thoroughfare, to the city centre.
Witnesses said mutineers then mingled with the civilian protesters to fire at sandbagged French positions in the avenue.
Mutineers used heavy-machine guns and grenades during sustained clashes which resumed in the afternoon until a storm restored calm. Mutineers returned to their original positions.

France has an estimated 2,000 troops stationed under a defence pact with the former French colony, whose main source of wealth is diamonds and where self-proclaimed emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa held sway from 1966 to 1979.

The mutinies began over pay but have turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a civilian elected in 1993 after the advent of multi-party politics. Patasse has refused to resign. Hundreds of people have died in violence associated with the revolts.
Four African leaders sent by a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in December negotiated a truce, which was extended until January 22, but tension and shootings have persisted.

Patasse, in a New Year broadcast to the nation, offered concessions -- amnesties for mutineers, creation of a committee of national reconciliation and a halt to judicial investigations into the activities of the administration of his pre-democracy predecessor, former military leader Andre Kolingba.
The mutineers remained unimpressed. Spokesmen repeated demands for Patasse to resign.
